resources.title: RICE Scoring
resources.summary: Prioritize initiatives by Reach, Impact, Confidence, and Effort with a single comparable score.

whenToUse: You need a defensible ranking to align stakeholders
whenNotToUse: Strategy-level bets where conviction beats arithmetic
steps: Sanity-check the top — does the order feel right?
outputs: A RICE score per item you can defend
mistakes: False precision — treat scores as directional
Gaming confidence to push pet projects
meta.example: A 12-item backlog: Feature B scores 42 (high reach, low effort) and beats Feature A at 18 — surfacing a non-obvious winner.

resources.title: ICE Scoring
resources.summary: A lightweight prioritization score from Impact, Confidence, and Ease — faster than RICE for quick calls.

whenNotToUse: Cross-team roadmap planning where effort varies wildly
meta.example: Onboarding tooltip: Impact 6, Confidence 8, Ease 9 → 7.7. Beats a risky pricing test at 4.3.

resources.title: Kano Model
resources.summary: Classify features by how they drive satisfaction: basic expectations, performance, and delighters.

whenToUse: Deciding which features actually move satisfaction
inputs: Functional + dysfunctional survey questions per feature
steps: Survey users on each feature present/absent
Fund all Basics, compete on Performance, sprinkle Delighters
outputs: Features sorted into Basic / Performance / Delighter / Indifferent
mistakes: Over-investing in delighters before basics are solid
Forgetting delighters decay into expectations over time
meta.example: For a banking app, fingerprint login moved from Delighter (2018) to Basic (2024).

resources.title: Jobs To Be Done
resources.summary: Frame products around the progress customers are trying to make, not demographics or features.

inputs: Customer interviews on a recent purchase/switch
steps: Write a job statement: When ___, I want to ___, so I can ___
mistakes: Too many jobs — pick the core one
meta.example: Milkshake bought for a boring commute (job: keep me occupied & full), competing with bananas and bagels — not other milkshakes.

resources.title: North Star Framework
resources.summary: Align the whole team behind one metric that captures the core value your product delivers.

whenNotToUse: As a vanity number with no input metrics
steps: Pick a metric that reflects delivered value
outputs: A North Star + input metric tree
meta.example: Spotify: time spent listening; inputs = activation, sessions/user, session length.

resources.title: AARRR (Pirate Metrics)
resources.summary: Map the user lifecycle across Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue to find the leak.

whenNotToUse: B2B with long sales cycles (adapt heavily)
steps: Define an event for each stage
outputs: A funnel with conversion rates per stage
meta.example: A SaaS with 40% signup→activation found onboarding, not ads, was the constraint.

resources.title: MoSCoW Prioritization
resources.summary: Scope a release by sorting requirements into Must, Should, Could, and Won't-have-now.

steps: Sort each into Must / Should / Could / Won't
Cap Musts to fit the timebox
mistakes: No Won't list to manage expectations
meta.example: An MVP launch with 4 Musts shipped on time; 6 Coulds moved to v1.1.

resources.title: Opportunity Solution Tree
resources.summary: Connect a desired outcome to opportunities, solutions, and experiments for continuous discovery.

whenNotToUse: One-off projects with a fixed solution
steps: Set the outcome at the root
Branch into experiments to test assumptions
outputs: A living tree linking work to outcomes
mistakes: Jumping to solutions before mapping opportunities
meta.example: Outcome: increase repeat orders → opportunity: 'I forget to reorder' → solution: reminders → experiment: SMS vs email.

resources.title: OKRs
resources.summary: Set an ambitious Objective with 3–5 measurable Key Results to focus and align a team.

whenNotToUse: As a task list or for individual performance reviews
steps: Check in weekly, grade at quarter end
mistakes: KRs that are tasks not outcomes
meta.example: O: Become the default for async standups. KR1: WAU 5k→12k. KR2: D30 retention 28%→40%.

resources.title: Working Backwards (PR/FAQ)
resources.summary: Start from a press release and FAQ for the finished product to force clarity before building.

steps: Write the launch press release first
Only build if the PR is compelling
mistakes: Writing it after deciding to build
meta.example: Amazon famously requires a PR/FAQ before greenlighting new products.

resources.title: Quarterly Planning Playbook
resources.summary: A repeatable four-week cadence to go from messy inputs to a committed, aligned quarterly plan.
resources.body:
## The cadence

A good quarterly plan is built, not announced. Run it as a four-week process so the plan arrives with buy-in already baked in.

## Week 1 — Inputs

Gather the raw material: last quarter's results, the current strategy, customer signals, and the top asks from sales, support, and leadership. Don't filter yet — just collect.

## Week 2 — Drafts

Write a draft set of objectives and the candidate initiatives under each. Score the initiatives with **RICE** to get a defensible starting order. Share the draft async for comment.

## Week 3 — Alignment

Pre-wire the plan one-on-one with each key stakeholder before any group meeting. Surface disagreements privately. By the time you present, there should be no surprises.

## Week 4 — Commit

Lock objectives and key results, name owners, and publish. Capacity-check: if everything is a priority, nothing is. Cut to fit.

## Anti-patterns

- Planning in a single marathon meeting.
- A plan with more objectives than the team can hold in its head.
- Treating the roadmap as a delivery contract instead of a statement of intent.

resources.title: Product Launch Playbook
resources.summary: Coordinate product, marketing, sales, and support to ship a launch that actually lands.
resources.body:
## Pick a launch tier

Not every release deserves a press tour. Decide up front: is this a **soft launch** (quiet, learn first), a **standard launch** (in-product + email), or a **tier-one launch** (full GTM motion)? Match the effort to the impact.

## Four weeks out — Foundations

Lock the positioning and the GTM brief. Define success metrics and confirm they're instrumented. Nothing ships unmeasured.

## Two weeks out — Enablement

Write the docs, brief support, and enable sales and CS with talking points and a demo. The people who talk to customers should hear about it before customers do.

## Launch week — Execute

Stage the in-product announcement, the email, and the external posts. Keep a rollback or kill switch ready. Watch the metrics dashboard in real time.

## After — Learn

Schedule the post-launch review before launch day so it actually happens. Compare results to the success metrics and capture what you'd do differently.

## The one rule

A launch is a beginning, not an ending. The work of driving adoption starts the day after.

resources.title: Continuous Discovery Playbook
resources.summary: Build a weekly habit of talking to customers so your roadmap stays grounded in real needs.
resources.body:
## The habit

Discovery isn't a phase — it's a weekly rhythm. The goal is a standing cadence of customer contact that continuously feeds your decisions.

## Set the outcome

Start every discovery cycle with a clear desired outcome, not a feature idea. Put it at the root of an **opportunity solution tree** so every interview maps back to it.

## Interview every week

Commit to at least one customer conversation per week as a team (PM, designer, engineer together). Consistency beats intensity — small, regular contact compounds.

## Map opportunities, not features

After each interview, add the unmet needs you heard to the tree as opportunities. Resist jumping to solutions until the opportunity space is clear.

## Test assumptions cheaply

For the solutions you do pursue, identify the riskiest assumption and design the smallest experiment that could disprove it. Build to learn, not to ship.

## Anti-patterns

- Batching all research into a quarterly 'discovery sprint.'
- Interviewing only when you already have a solution to validate.
- A tree no one looks at after the workshop.

resources.title: How to Write a PRD That Engineers Actually Read
resources.summary: A practical method for writing requirements docs that drive alignment instead of gathering dust.
resources.body:
## The PRD's only job

A PRD exists to create shared understanding and unblock decisions — not to specify every pixel. If your doc isn't reducing ambiguity, it's overhead.

## Start with the problem, not the solution

Open with **who** has the problem, **what** the pain is today, and **evidence** it's real. If you can't cite an interview, a ticket trend, or a metric, you're guessing.

## Make goals falsifiable

Write success metrics you could actually fail. "Improve onboarding" is a wish; "lift signup→activation from 38% to 50%" is a goal.

## Keep requirements thin

List what must be true, not how to build it. Trust your engineers on implementation — over-specifying invites resentment and removes their judgment.

## Name the non-goals

The fastest way to prevent scope creep is an explicit *Non-goals* section. It's permission to say no later without re-litigating.

## Close with risks and open questions

A confident PRD that hides its uncertainties is fragile. Surfacing risks early is what senior PMs do.

## A good rhythm

Draft → share async for comments → 30-min walkthrough → decisions logged → build. The doc is a conversation, not a contract.

resources.title: How to Choose a North Star Metric
resources.summary: Pick and pressure-test the single metric that reflects the value your product delivers.
resources.body:
## What a North Star is (and isn't)

It's the single metric that best captures the value customers get from your product. It is **not** revenue — revenue is the result of delivering value, not the value itself.

## Three tests for a good North Star

1. **Value test** — does it go up when customers genuinely succeed?
2. **Leading test** — does it predict future revenue/retention?
3. **Actionable test** — can teams actually move it?

## Decompose it into inputs

A North Star you can't break into inputs is a poster, not a system. Spotify's "time spent listening" decomposes into activation, sessions per user, and session length — each ownable by a team.

## Add guardrails

Every North Star can be gamed. Pair it with guardrail metrics (e.g. unsubscribe rate, support tickets) so teams don't win the metric while losing the customer.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing a vanity number (page views).
- Choosing a lagging result (ARR) with no inputs.
- Changing it every quarter — it should be stable for years.

resources.title: Running Discovery Interviews Without Leading the Witness
resources.summary: How to interview customers so you learn the truth instead of confirming your bias.
resources.body:
## Ask about the past, not the future

People are terrible at predicting what they'll do and great at recalling what they did. Replace "Would you use X?" with "Tell me about the last time you faced this."

## Hunt for the struggling moment

The richest signal is the moment of struggle that triggered a search for a solution. Anchor every interview on a specific recent instance.

## Shut up

The most common mistake is talking. Aim for an 80/20 split — they talk, you listen. Silence pulls out the real answer.

## Watch for emotion

When someone gets animated, slow down and dig. Emotion marks where the real job lives.

## Never pitch

The second you describe your solution, the interview is over — they'll be polite, not honest.

resources.title: Prioritization in Practice
resources.summary: Move beyond scoring formulas to make prioritization calls that survive contact with reality.
resources.body:
## Frameworks are inputs, not verdicts

RICE gives you a starting order, not a decision. Use the score to spark the conversation, then apply judgment about strategy, sequencing, and dependencies.

## Separate the two questions

"Is this worth doing?" and "Is this worth doing *now*?" are different. Many good ideas are simply mistimed.

## Make the cost of delay visible

The strongest prioritization argument is often what you lose by waiting — not the upside of acting.

## Protect a discovery budget

If 100% of capacity goes to delivery, you'll run out of validated ideas. Reserve ~20% for discovery.

resources.title: Stakeholder Management for PMs
resources.summary: Build trust and alignment across leadership, engineering, design, and go-to-market.
resources.body:
## Map before you manage

List your stakeholders and rate each on influence and interest. You manage a high-influence skeptic very differently from a supportive bystander.

## No surprises

The core rule of stakeholder trust: leaders should never hear bad news first in a public forum. Pre-wire decisions one-on-one.

## Translate, don't transmit

The same update should sound different to a CFO (cost, risk) and an engineer (scope, tradeoffs). Tailor the framing, keep the facts identical.

## Disagree and commit, visibly

When a call goes against you, support it publicly. Re-litigating in the hallway destroys trust faster than any wrong decision.

resources.title: Setting OKRs That Actually Work
resources.summary: Avoid the common traps that turn OKRs into a quarterly box-ticking ritual.
resources.body:
## Outcomes, not output

The number-one OKR failure: key results that are really tasks. "Ship the new dashboard" is output. "Increase weekly active teams 20%" is an outcome.

## Fewer, bolder

One objective and 3–5 key results per team. More than that and focus evaporates.

## Set a baseline

A target without a baseline is unmeasurable. Always write current → target.

## Decouple from comp

The moment OKRs drive bonuses, people sandbag. Keep them aspirational; grade ~0.7 as a healthy stretch.

resources.title: Activation: The Most Important Funnel Step
resources.summary: Find your product's aha moment and engineer more users toward it, faster.
resources.body:
## Why activation beats acquisition

Pouring users into a product that doesn't activate is lighting money on fire. Activation is usually the highest-leverage point in the funnel.

## Find the aha moment

Look for the action that correlates with long-term retention. Facebook's was famously "7 friends in 10 days." Find yours by comparing retained vs churned cohorts.

## Define a setup moment + aha moment

Users need to reach a *setup* state (e.g. connected data) before they can hit the *aha*. Map both and reduce friction to each.

## Measure time-to-value

The faster a new user reaches value, the more activate. Track median time-to-aha and drive it down.

resources.title: Using AI in Your PM Workflow
resources.summary: Concrete ways to use LLMs for discovery synthesis, drafting, and analysis — with the guardrails.
resources.body:
## Where AI genuinely helps a PM

- **Synthesis**: paste 20 interview notes, ask for recurring jobs and surprising quotes.
- **Drafting**: turn a rough PRD outline into prose you then sharpen.
- **Analysis**: explain a SQL result, draft a query, sanity-check a metric definition.
- **Devil's advocate**: ask it to argue against your strategy.

## The guardrails

- Never paste confidential customer data into tools without approval.
- Treat output as a fast first draft, never a source of truth.
- Verify every number and citation it produces.

## A prompt pattern that works

Give it a role, the context, the format you want, and an example. Specificity beats cleverness.

meta.example: Sean Ellis test: ≥40% of users would be 'very disappointed' without your product.

resources.title: Minimum Viable Product
resources.summary: The smallest version of a product that lets you validate a core hypothesis with real users.

meta.example: Dropbox's MVP was a demo video, not a working product.

resources.title: Customer Acquisition Cost
resources.summary: The total sales and marketing cost to acquire one new customer.

meta.example: $40,000 spend ÷ 200 new customers = $200 CAC.

resources.title: Lifetime Value
resources.summary: The total gross profit you expect from a customer across their entire relationship.

meta.example: Healthy SaaS targets an LTV:CAC ratio of roughly 3:1 or better.

resources.title: Churn
resources.summary: The rate at which customers (logo churn) or revenue (revenue churn) leave over a period.

meta.example: 5% monthly logo churn ≈ losing half your customers in ~14 months.

resources.title: Activation
resources.summary: The moment a new user first experiences the product's core value (the 'aha moment').

meta.example: Slack: a team sending 2,000 messages.

resources.title: Retention
resources.summary: The share of users who keep coming back over time — the truest signal of delivered value.

meta.example: A flattening retention curve (not decaying to zero) signals product-market fit.

resources.title: TAM / SAM / SOM

meta.example: TAM: all coffee drinkers; SAM: those near your city; SOM: those you can realistically serve year one.

resources.title: CAC Calculator
resources.summary: Work out your customer acquisition cost from sales & marketing spend and new customers.

meta.note: CAC = total sales & marketing spend ÷ new customers acquired in the same period.

resources.body:
## What it tells you

Customer acquisition cost is the fully-loaded price of winning one new customer. Read it alongside **LTV** — CAC alone is only half the story.

## Watch outs

- Include *all* go-to-market cost (salaries, tools, ads), not just ad spend.
- Use the same time window for spend and customers.
- Segment by channel — blended CAC hides your best and worst channels.

resources.title: LTV Calculator
resources.summary: Estimate customer lifetime value from ARPU, gross margin, and monthly churn.

meta.note: LTV = (ARPU × gross margin) ÷ monthly churn rate. Lifespan = 1 ÷ churn.

resources.body:
## What it tells you

Lifetime value is the gross profit you can expect from an average customer. Margin matters — revenue LTV flatters a low-margin business.

## Watch outs

- Use gross-margin LTV, not revenue LTV, for any CAC comparison.
- Churn-based LTV assumes a steady churn rate; for early-stage products it's a rough estimate.

resources.title: LTV : CAC Ratio Calculator
resources.summary: Check whether your unit economics work by comparing lifetime value to acquisition cost.

meta.note: LTV:CAC = LTV ÷ CAC. ~3:1 is the common health benchmark; much higher can mean under-investment in growth.

resources.body:
## What it tells you

The single fastest read on whether growth is sustainable. Below 3:1, acquisition is likely too expensive; far above 3:1, you may be leaving growth on the table by under-spending.

resources.title: CAC Payback Calculator
resources.summary: How many months until a new customer pays back what it cost to acquire them.

meta.note: Payback (months) = CAC ÷ (ARPU × gross margin). Under ~12 months is generally efficient for SaaS.

resources.body:
## What it tells you

Payback period is a cash-flow lens on acquisition. Even with a great LTV:CAC, a long payback strains a young company's runway.

resources.title: RICE Score Calculator
resources.summary: Score a single initiative on Reach, Impact, Confidence, and Effort.

meta.note: RICE = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort. Score one item, then repeat to rank a backlog.

resources.body:
## What it tells you

A single comparable number for an initiative. Scores are directional — use them to start the prioritization conversation, not to end it.

resources.title: Funnel Conversion Calculator
resources.summary: See how visitors flow through signup, activation, and paid — and your overall conversion.

meta.note: Each stage multiplies the last. Overall conversion = paying customers ÷ visitors.

resources.body:
## What it tells you

Where your funnel leaks. Multiply the stage rates and the compounding effect makes the biggest drop-off obvious — fix that one first.

resources.title: Runway Calculator
resources.summary: How many months of cash you have left at your current burn rate.

meta.note: Runway (months) = cash ÷ net monthly burn. Most teams start fundraising with 6–9 months left.

resources.body:
## What it tells you

How long you can operate before you need more cash. Founders doing PM work should keep this number visible — it shapes every prioritization call.

resources.title: TAM / SAM / SOM Calculator
resources.summary: Size a market top-down from total customers, ACV, and your serviceable and obtainable shares.

meta.note: TAM = customers × ACV. SAM = TAM × serviceable %. SOM = SAM × obtainable %.

resources.body:
## What it tells you

A quick top-down market size. Treat it as a sanity check, not gospel — pair it with a bottoms-up estimate before betting a strategy on it.

resources.title: How Slack Grew Bottoms-Up
resources.summary: A teardown of Slack's product-led, team-by-team go-to-market and the activation metric behind it.
resources.body:
## Context

Slack entered a crowded chat market by targeting teams, not companies — landing inside one team and expanding outward.

## The key decision

Slack defined activation as a team sending **2,000 messages** — the point where habit formed. Everything in onboarding pushed toward that threshold.

## Outcome

Bottoms-up adoption created internal champions who pulled in IT, collapsing the enterprise sales cycle.

## Lessons

- A precise activation metric focuses the whole funnel.
- Land in a team, expand to the org.
- Word-of-mouth is a product feature, not just marketing.

resources.title: Superhuman's PMF Engine
resources.summary: How Superhuman turned the fuzzy idea of product-market fit into a measurable, improvable system.
resources.body:
## Context

Superhuman struggled to know if they had product-market fit, so they made it measurable.

## The key decision

They surveyed users: 'How would you feel if you could no longer use Superhuman?' and tracked the **% who said 'very disappointed.'** They focused the roadmap on converting the 'somewhat disappointed' segment.

## Outcome

The metric climbed past the 40% benchmark, and the method became a widely-copied PMF playbook.

## Lessons

- You can instrument PMF, not just feel it.
- Segment your users and improve the ones on the edge.
- A single recurring question can anchor a roadmap.

resources.title: Duolingo's Retention Machine
resources.summary: How streaks, notifications, and gamification rebuilt Duolingo's retention curve.
resources.body:
## Context

Duolingo's growth stalled until they treated retention as the core product problem.

## The key decision

They rebuilt around the **streak** — a simple, emotionally loaded commitment device — and ruthlessly optimized notifications with experimentation.

## Outcome

DAU growth reaccelerated dramatically, driven by retention rather than acquisition.

## Lessons

- Retention compounds; acquisition leaks.
- Emotional mechanics (streaks, loss aversion) outperform feature lists.
- A relentless experimentation culture turns small wins into a curve shift.

resources.title: The CIRCLES Method
resources.summary: A structured framework for answering product design questions in interviews.
resources.body:
## CIRCLES

A repeatable structure for 'design a product' interview questions:

- **C**omprehend the situation — clarify scope and constraints.
- **I**dentify the customer — pick a segment.
- **R**eport the customer's needs — list jobs and pains.
- **C**ut through prioritization — pick the needs to solve.
- **L**ist solutions — brainstorm broadly.
- **E**valuate tradeoffs — compare options.
- **S**ummarize your recommendation — commit to one.

## Why it works

Interviewers grade structure and judgment, not cleverness. CIRCLES keeps you from jumping straight to features and shows a defensible process.
